summary:
01. HIGH-LEVEL SUMMARY

MADAR is an educational web game that lets anyone design a space mission and fly it, from the first decision to the landing back on Earth. It meets the Space Mission Design Game challenge by turning real mission-design constraints (budget, mass, fuel, power, radiation, launch windows and risk) into choices the player must make and live with. The player takes a crew role, chooses a science goal and a destination, builds a launch vehicle and spacecraft, launches in a physics-based simulator, survives the journey, and receives a full mission report after landing.

Mission design is normally reserved for specialists, and real experience costs millions of dollars and years of work. MADAR makes it accessible to students and enthusiasts, who learn by doing and can fail at no cost. It can be played alone or in teams of up to four, where each player gets the role that fits them best. It matters because it helps train future space engineers and planners and makes 
NASA’s open data easy to understand through play
details:
How it works

  1. Main menu. The player chooses single-player or multiplayer (up to 4 players). In single-player, the player makes every decision, from mission design to the landing back on Earth.
  2. Crew onboarding and roles. Each player answers 7 scenario questions: budget vs. ambition, risk tolerance, love of detail, communication style, data vs. intuition, leadership vs. specialist, and calm under pressure. The answers score four roles: Mission Commander / Project Manager, Systems Engineer, Science Lead, and Comms & Flight Ops. The game recommends the best match with a percentage, and the player can still choose another role. Each role controls different decisions and conflicts with others, as on a real team. The player then creates a Crew ID with a skill profile.
  3. Mission design. The player first chooses a scientific goal, following NASA’s concept-maturity principle that science objectives come before hardware. The player then chooses one of 17 destinations: LEO, GEO, HEO, Moon, Mars, Phobos, Deimos, Vesta, Ceres, Venus, Jupiter, Europa, Titan, the Sun, Sun–Earth L1, Sun–Earth L2, and the magnetosphere. Each destination shows real values such as gravity, radiation dose, communication delay, solar flux and delta-v. The game sizes the vehicle with the rocket equation, m₀ = m_dry · exp(Δv / (Isp · g₀)), so every choice has a real consequence.
  4. Vehicle builder. The player assembles the launch vehicle and spacecraft from real engines and propellants (for example Merlin Vacuum, RS-25, RD-180 and RL10C-1, using kerosene, hydrogen or storable propellants). The rocket cost updates live, and each part explains its trade-offs.
  5. Propulsion strategies. The player chooses how to fuel the trip:
    • Carry all the fuel for the whole round trip.
    • Make fuel at the destination. The player carries only the fuel needed to get there and produces the return propellant on site. This works only on destinations where the chemistry is possible, such as a CO₂ atmosphere. The game models these reactions:
      • Sabatier reactor: CO₂ + 4H₂ → CH₄ + 2H₂O, at about 300–400 °C over a nickel catalyst, releasing heat.
      • Water electrolysis: 2H₂O → 2H₂ + O₂. The oxygen goes to the tank, and the hydrogen is fed back to the Sabatier reactor.
      • CO₂ splitter (MOXIE type): 2CO₂ → 2CO + O₂, at about 800 °C, with the carbon monoxide vented.
      • Net result of the Sabatier reaction and electrolysis: CO₂ + 2H₂ → CH₄ + O₂. In the engine: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O.
  6. Launch windows and launch. The player must respect real launch windows (Moon about every 27 days, Mars about every 26 months, where missing a Mars window costs about two years). The launch runs in Helios Ascent, a 3D simulator based on published Falcon 9-class masses, thrust and specific impulse, the 1976 U.S. Standard Atmosphere, and a fixed-step physics integrator. Random anomalies can occur, such as engine thrust loss, a propellant leak, a structural failure or an upper-stage failure, so a badly designed rocket can fail at launch.
  7. Journey, events and landing. The mission passes through phases: waiting for the window, launch, orbit insertion, cruise, entry, landing and operations. Radiation dose, communication delay and solar flux are tracked continuously, and random accidents can happen on the way to and from the destination. For surface missions, a Surface Base Builder lets the player plan habitat and power layouts.
  8. Mission report. After a safe landing on Earth, a full report shows the overall success rate, whether the mission purpose was achieved, and the good and bad decisions the player made.

Benefits

  • Education. Players learn real mission engineering: science goals, budget, mass, power, fuel, radiation and risk.
  • Low cost. It gives hands-on mission-design experience that would otherwise cost far more.
  • Teamwork. Role-based multiplayer for up to four players, with conflicting priorities as in a real mission team.
  • Safe failure. Players learn from mistakes, and the report explains them.
  • Classroom use. A teacher can run the game with a class and compare the mission reports of different teams.
  • Accessible data. NASA open data becomes understandable through play.

Tools and languages
JavaScript, HTML and CSS; React and Vite (application); Three.js (3D rendering and launch simulator); Zustand (state management); Framer Motion (animation); Google Fonts (Space Grotesk, JetBrains Mono, Barlow).

Limits
The launch model is a simplified educational model. It is not flight-certified and does not predict any real launch. Game-balance values are labelled as such and are never presented as NASA measurements.
